body: Oman mostly features a desert landscape. The north coast has dry mountains similar to the UAE, while the south coast mountains are less dry. The middle and southern half is mostly flat.
Private vehicles in Oman generally have yellow licence plates, while commercial vehicles have red plates.
All coverage in Oman was captured using a white pickup truck, meaning you will often see the car itself or a large front blur.
The official language in Oman is Arabic. However, due to tourism, signs often include English, a practice also common in the UAE.
Roads in Oman use yellow outer lines and white middle lines. This is also common in several neighboring countries.
Black-and-yellow curbs are common in Oman, similar to the UAE.

Buildings in Oman are typically ornate, ‘blocky’ structures made of light-coloured stone, often surrounded by a matching fence with an even more ornate gate. This architecture is very similar to that found in the UAE.
Directional signs are blue with white text and are usually in both Arabic and English. The UAE and Qatar use similar signs.
Many signposts in Oman have black-and-white stripes. Within the Middle East, this feature is only shared with the UAE.
Oman frequently uses wooden poles, more so than the UAE or Qatar. A unique design to look for is a poletop with a metal triangle above the wooden pole.
Oman uses distinctive black-and-yellow chevrons that feature an unusually large number of arrows.
High voltage pylons painted with a red and white pattern are common in Oman. They can also be found less frequently in Qatar.
The majority of garbage bins in Oman feature a three-leaf logo and the text ‘be’ah’. In contrast, bins in the UAE might say “bee’ah” and are often more colourful.
Taxis in Oman are white and have orange-coloured panels on each side.
Northern Oman has a dry mountainous landscape similar to that of the eastern UAE.
Near the southern coast, especially around Salalah, you will find a landscape of rolling hills. This area often has rocky ground, bushes, small trees, and some fairly green valleys.

The mountains north of Nizwa have an unusually large amount of green bushes for the north. These mountains are very rocky and jagged, which differentiates them from the more rolling mountains in the south.
A sandy desert with light coloured green and yellow shrubs can be found in northeastern Oman, mainly south and west of Bidiyah.
South of Bidiyah, some dirt roads run through a slightly rolling landscape of orange-pink sand and small yellowish shrubs, typically between long, low sand dunes.
Salalah is situated on a flat coastal plain with rolling mountains to its north.
Masirah Island is dry and slightly hilly, with somewhat grey soil and brown shrubs. Road 51 on the island often has only a white centre line, and the front camera view is slightly smudged.
Acacia trees, known for their short height and umbrella-like flat crowns, are most common in northern Oman but can be found near other coastal areas as well.
Date palm plantations are most common along the northern coast, while coconut palms are typically found near Salalah.
The colour of garbage bins in Oman can help narrow down your location, although some regions have a mix of colours.
Many bins have a set of numbers that can identify the region. The first pair of numbers indicates the governorate.
Black bins with a black sticker on the front are found in the Al Buraimi, Ash Sharqiyah North, and Muscat Governorates.
Grey bins with a black sticker on the front are found in the Ad Dhahirah Governorate.
Black bins with a white sticker are found in the Ad Dakhiliyah Governorate, southern Dhofar Governorate, and Muscat Governorate.
Grey bins with a white sticker are commonly found in the Ad Dakhiliyah Governorate and sometimes in the Dhofar Governorate.

Black bins without stickers are mainly found in the Al Batinah South Governorate and north of Al Khaburah in the Al Batinah North Governorate. Use this clue with caution, as stickers may be missing elsewhere.
Grey bins without a sticker on the front are found in the Al Batinah North Governorate, although they may have a sticker on the side.
Western-style small black bins are found in Muscat and the eastern Al Batinah North Governorate.
Bins in the Muscat governorate often have white-and-red chevron-like stickers on the sides.
Regardless of colour, if a bin has a sticker on the side, you are likely in one of the North Coast governorates.
An antenna bent to the right is found all over the south and in a few pockets in the north.
An antenna that is facing towards the camera is found all over the north.
A regular-looking antenna that faces upwards is mainly found around and west of Muscat, and on highways in the northwest.
A forwards-facing antenna is only found in and around Muscat.

A backwards-facing antenna can indicate smaller regions based on the wire on its bar. For example, no wire is in the northwest, a looping wire is around Al Suwayq, and a small looping wire is mainly in the east.
Two clearly visible zip-ties can be found on a few roads in the southwest, notably on most of Road 39 and southern Road 43.
Just north of Adam, you'll find a flat desert with greyish soil and mountains in the distance. Look for a long ridge to the south and two smaller, rounder hills to the east and southeast.
In and close to Adam, the coverage is often hazy. The ridge and hills mentioned previously can be seen to the north, but you won’t see mountains in any other direction.
Around the town of Ubar, you can find patches of green agricultural land surrounded by desert.
Oil drills are common around Amal and can sometimes be seen along Road 39.
If you are in a somewhat urban area and surrounded by mountains on all sides, you are likely in Al Amarat, just southeast of Muscat.
Most coverage in the Musandam Governorate exclave is coastal, with rocky cliffs hugging the road. A majority of this coverage will have the coast to the west.
A road going through large orange-pink sand dunes can be found north of Fasad. These same dunes can be seen in the distance near the northern part of the Yemen border.
The road to Saudi Arabia from Ibri can be recognized by its completely flat desert landscape with bright pink-greyish soil, very wide shoulders, and excellent condition.
The road west of Fahud also goes through a flat desert with pink-greyish soil, but it is in poor shape and lacks roadlines.
Road 29 south of Ibri has a fairly shrubby landscape, with low, jagged mountains to the east. The low-lying sun to the northwest is a particularly distinct feature.
The southern section of Road 29 is unique for having only a middle white line in a greyish, sandy desert landscape.
A long stretch of Road 31 can be identified by its light-coloured flat desert landscape, wide shoulders, and often faded road lines under somewhat cloudy weather.
The divided section of Road 31 is the only divided road in the coverage that goes through a flat desert landscape.
The southernmost section of Road 32 has a somewhat hilly landscape. The puffy cumulus clouds are what really sets this road apart.
